label: thm:main-interval
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main-interval}
For \(\mathbb K=\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb K=\mathbb C\),
\[
        d_{\mathrm{BM}}(X_\mathbb K,Y_\mathbb K)
        \leqslant (2+\sqrt5)^2=9+4\sqrt5=17.944\ldots
\]
head: environment

label: thm:kernel-absorption-main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:kernel-absorption-main}
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be non-zero Banach spaces over \(\mathbb K\).  Suppose that \(P\) is a norm-one projection on \(X\) such that \(P[X]\) is isometric to \(Y\) and \(E=\ker P\) is isomorphic to \(X\).  Suppose also that \(R\) is a norm-one projection on \(Y\) such that \(R[Y]\) is isometric to \(X\), and that \(X\) is isometric to \(X\oplus_\infty X\).  If \(\rho=\|I_X-P\|\) and \(\sigma=\|I_Y-R\|\), then
\[
        d_{\mathrm{BM}}(X,Y)\leqslant \bigl(\sigma+\sqrt{\rho\,d_{\mathrm{BM}}(E,X)+1}\bigr)^2.
\]
In particular, \(d_{\mathrm{BM}}(X,Y)\leqslant \bigl(2+\sqrt{2\,d_{\mathrm{BM}}(E,X)+1}\bigr)^2\).
head: environment

label: lem:T-bijection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:T-bijection}
The operator \(T\) is a bijection of \(X\) onto \(Y\), and
\[
        \|T\|\leqslant\max\{\rho\alpha\|A\|,\beta\}+\sigma\gamma,
        \qquad
        \|T^{-1}\|\leqslant \frac{\|A^{-1}\|}{\alpha}+\frac1\beta+\frac\sigma\gamma .
\]
head: environment

label: eq:S
title: Proof
body_md:
We use \(P\eta=\eta\) and \(R\theta=\theta\).  Define \(S\colon Y\to X\) by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S}
Sz=\eta\left(\theta\left(\frac1\beta\pi_2\Phi\theta^{-1}Rz\right)+\frac1\gamma(I_Y-R)z\right)+\frac1\alpha A^{-1}\pi_1\Phi\theta^{-1}Rz .
\end{equation}
We show that \(S=T^{-1}\).

Fix \(x\in X\) and write \(e=(I_X-P)x\), \(y=\eta^{-1}Px\), \(u=\theta^{-1}Ry\) and \(f=(I_Y-R)y\).  Then \(Tx=\theta\Phi^{-1}(\alpha Ae,\beta u)+\gamma f\).  Since \(R\theta=\theta\) and \(Rf=0\), one has \(RTx=\theta\Phi^{-1}(\alpha Ae,\beta u)\) and \((I_Y-R)Tx=\gamma f\).  Hence \(\Phi\theta^{-1}RTx=(\alpha Ae,\beta u)\), and the three pieces decoded by \(S\) are precisely \(e\), \(u\) and \(f\).  The expression inside the parentheses in \eqref{eq:S}, evaluated at \(Tx\), is therefore \(\theta u+f=Ry+(I_Y-R)y=y\), and so \(STx=\eta y+e=x\).

Conversely, fix \(z\in Y\) and write \(w=\theta^{-1}Rz\), \((v_1,v_2)=\Phi w\), \(e=\alpha^{-1}A^{-1}v_1\), \(u=\beta^{-1}v_2\), \(f=\gamma^{-1}(I_Y-R)z\) and \(y=\theta u+f\).  Then \(Sz=\eta y+e\).  Since \(P\eta=\eta\) and \(Pe=0\), we have \(PSz=\eta y\), \(\eta^{-1}PSz=y\) and \((I_X-P)Sz=e\).  Since \(R\theta=\theta\) and \(Rf=0\), we also have \(Ry=\theta u\), \(\theta^{-1}R\eta^{-1}PSz=u\) and \((I_Y-R)\eta^{-1}PSz=f\).  Thus \(TSz=\theta\Phi^{-1}(v_1,v_2)+(I_Y-R)z=\theta w+(I_Y-R)z=z\).

It remains only to estimate the two norms.  If \(\|x\|\leqslant1\) and the notation from the first paragraph is used, then \(\|e\|\leqslant\rho\), \(\|y\|\leqslant1\), \(\|u\|\leqslant1\) and \(\|f\|\leqslant\sigma\).  Since \(\theta\) and \(\Phi^{-1}\) are isometries and \(X\oplus_\infty X\) has the maximum norm, this gives \(\|Tx\|\leqslant\max\{\rho\alpha\|A\|,\beta\}+\sigma\gamma\).  Similarly, if \(\|z\|\leqslant1\), then \(\|w\|\leqslant1\) and \(\max\{\|v_1\|,\|v_2\|\}\leqslant1\), so \(\|e\|\leqslant\|A^{-1}\|/\alpha\), \(\|u\|\leqslant1/\beta\) and \(\|f\|\leqslant\sigma/\gamma\).  Hence \(\|Sz\|\leqslant\|A^{-1}\|/\alpha+1/\beta+\sigma/\gamma\).

label: lem:optimisation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:optimisation}
If \(c,\rho,\sigma>0\), then
\[
\inf_{a,\beta,\gamma>0}\left(\max\{\rho a,\beta\}+\sigma\gamma\right)\left(\frac ca+\frac1\beta+\frac\sigma\gamma\right)=\bigl(\sigma+\sqrt{\rho c+1}\bigr)^2.
\]
The infimum is attained, up to homogeneous scaling, for \(a=t\), \(\beta=\rho t\) and \(\gamma=\rho t/\sqrt{\rho c+1}\), where \(t>0\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(G(a,\beta,\gamma)\) denote the expression being minimised, and put \(m=\max\{\rho a,\beta\}\).  Replacing \((a,\beta)\) by \((m/\rho,m)\) leaves the first factor equal to \(m+\sigma\gamma\).  Since \(m/\rho\geqslant a\) and \(m\geqslant\beta\), and since \(c/a+1/\beta+\sigma/\gamma\) is decreasing separately in \(a\) and \(\beta\), the second factor cannot increase.  Thus the infimum is attained on the slice \(\beta=\rho a\).

On that slice,
\[
G(a,\rho a,\gamma)=(\rho a+\sigma\gamma)\left(\frac ca+\frac1{\rho a}+\frac\sigma\gamma\right)
=\rho c+1+\sigma^2+\frac{\rho\sigma a}{\gamma}+\frac{\sigma\gamma(c+1/\rho)}{a}.
\]
The last two terms have product \(\sigma^2(\rho c+1)\); hence their sum is at least \(2\sigma\sqrt{\rho c+1}\).  This gives \(G(a,\rho a,\gamma)\geqslant (\sigma+\sqrt{\rho c+1})^2\), and equality holds precisely when \(\rho a/\gamma=\gamma(c+1/\rho)/a\), that is, when \(\gamma=\rho a/\sqrt{\rho c+1}\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If \(\sigma=0\), then \(R=I_Y\) and the isometry \(\theta\colon X\to Y\) gives \(d_{\mathrm{BM}}(X,Y)=1\).  We may therefore assume that \(\sigma>0\).  Since \(E\cong X\) and \(X\ne0\), the projection \(P\) is not the identity, so \(\rho>0\).

Choose \(A\colon E\to X\) with \(\|A\|\|A^{-1}\|<d_{\mathrm{BM}}(E,X)+\varepsilon\).  Lemma~\ref{lem:T-bijection}, followed by Lemma~\ref{lem:optimisation} with \(a=\alpha\|A\|\), gives \(d_{\mathrm{BM}}(X,Y)\leqslant (\sigma+\sqrt{\rho(d_{\mathrm{BM}}(E,X)+\varepsilon)+1})^2\).  Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves the first assertion, and the second follows from \(\rho,\sigma\leqslant2\).
head: environment

label: rem:threshold
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:threshold}
For norm-one projections the estimate reads \(d_{\mathrm{BM}}(X,Y)\leqslant (2+\sqrt{2c+1})^2\), where \(c=d_{\mathrm{BM}}(E,X)\).  This improves the previously available constant \(9+6\sqrt3\) whenever \(c<6+3\sqrt3-2\sqrt{9+6\sqrt3}=2.389\).  Thus the estimate \(c\leqslant2\) obtained below has some room.  One alternative route would be to improve the complement norm of a projection from \(L_\infty\) onto an isometric copy of \(\ell_\infty\); for orientation, it has been observed in a MathOverflow discussion that this should not be expected in that form \cite{ComplementConstantMO}.  This observation is not used in the proof.

label: thm:cohen-bound-two
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cohen-bound-two}
For \(\mathbb K=\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb K=\mathbb C\), there are distinct points \(p,q\in K\) such that, if \(K_{p\sim q}\) is obtained from \(K\) by identifying \(p\) and \(q\), then
\[
        d_{\mathrm{BM}}\bigl(C(K;\mathbb K),C(K_{p\sim q};\mathbb K)\bigr)\leqslant2.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This is the two-point case of Cohen's bound-two construction.  In Cohen's paper \cite[pp.~215--217]{Cohen1975} the isomorphism is given by its dual representation, with point masses and two-point measures as representing measures, and it has norm \(1\) with inverse norm at most \(2\) after rescaling.  The formula uses only real coefficients in the representing measures, and therefore gives a \(\mathbb K\)-linear operator on \(\mathbb K\)-valued continuous functions for both \(\mathbb K=\mathbb R\) and \(\mathbb K=\mathbb C\).  A topological formulation of the same bound-two phenomenon is given by Cohen--Chu \cite[Section~3, Theorem]{CohenChu}, where a finite bridge relation between compact Hausdorff spaces is shown to be equivalent to the existence of a bound-two isomorphism between the corresponding real \(C(K)\) spaces.

For the present application the component compacta in Cohen's construction are taken to be non-empty clopen pieces of the Stone space of the Lebesgue measure algebra.  This is legitimate because every non-empty clopen piece of \(K\) is again homeomorphic to \(K\): indeed, it is the Stone space associated with the restriction of a non-zero continuous finite measure, and the resulting character space is homeomorphic to \(\Phi_\mu\) by the measure-algebra isomorphism theorem recalled in \cite[Theorem~2.19 and Corollary~2.20]{DalesLauStrauss}.  With the two distinguished endpoints denoted by \(p\) and \(q\), the compactum on one side of Cohen's construction is homeomorphic to \(K\), and the one on the other side is homeomorphic to the quotient \(K_{p\sim q}\).

label: thm:upper
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:upper}
For \(\mathbb K=\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb K=\mathbb C\), one has \(d_{\mathrm{BM}}(X_\mathbb K,Y_\mathbb K)\leqslant (2+\sqrt5)^2=9+4\sqrt5=17.944\ldots\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:kernel-absorption-main} with \(X=X_\mathbb K\), \(Y=Y_\mathbb K\), \(\rho,\sigma\leqslant2\) and \(d_{\mathrm{BM}}(E,X_\mathbb K)\leqslant2\).

label: prop:cylindrical
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:cylindrical}
For every such pair \((M,L)\), \(F(M)I(L)\geqslant\rho c+1\).  Equality is attained by the diagonal two-coordinate code \(M(q,u)=(q/\rho,u)\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By homogeneity it suffices to consider \(F(M)\leqslant1\).  If \(r_j=(m_{j1},m_{j2})\) is the \(j\)th row of \(M\), then every \(r_j\) belongs to the diamond \(D_\rho=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb K^2:\rho|s|+|t|\leqslant1\}\).  Its Minkowski functional is \(p_{D_\rho}(s,t)=\rho|s|+|t|\).  Since \(LM=I_2\), the coordinate vectors satisfy \(e_1=\sum_j\ell_{1j}r_j\) and \(e_2=\sum_j\ell_{2j}r_j\).  By subadditivity of \(p_{D_\rho}\), one has \(\sum_j|\ell_{1j}|\geqslant p_{D_\rho}(e_1)=\rho\) and \(\sum_j|\ell_{2j}|\geqslant p_{D_\rho}(e_2)=1\).  Hence \(I(L)\geqslant c\rho+1\) when \(F(M)\leqslant1\), and the general case follows by scaling \(M\).  Equality is obtained from \(M=\operatorname{diag}(1/\rho,1)\) and \(L=\operatorname{diag}(\rho,1)\).
head: environment

label: cor:cylindrical
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:cylindrical}
After the unabsorbed \(F\)-kernel term is added with parameter \(\gamma>0\), every finite scalar code in the preceding model gives at least \(\bigl(\sigma+\sqrt{\rho c+1}\bigr)^2\), and the diagonal two-coordinate code attains equality.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For fixed positive \(F\) and \(I\), \(\inf_{\gamma>0}(F+\sigma\gamma)(I+\sigma/\gamma)=(\sigma+\sqrt{FI})^2\).  Proposition~\ref{prop:cylindrical} gives \(FI\geqslant\rho c+1\).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The r\^ole of the reverse kernel \(F=\ker R\) is thus only to contribute the two terms \(\sigma\gamma\) and \(\sigma/\gamma\) in the forward and inverse estimates.  The absorbed kernel \(E=\ker P\) contributes through \(\rho c\), while the range coordinate contributes the additional \(1\).
